asof: This is a weekend edition, and that makes it cleaner than the last two. Every price and percentage on both sheets is a genuine closing print from Friday, Aug 7, and every positioning column (30-day range position, vs 50-day, distribution days, heavy liquidation events, volume ratio) and every number in the Quant Lab is computed from that same completed session. For once the price column and the flow columns describe the same moment, so you can read them together without adjusting for a timing gap. Friday was a record close: the S&P 500 rose 0.62% to 7,757.64, the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.30% to 26,690.62 and the Dow added 0.28% to 54,036.93, capping the strongest week since April (S&P up 3.58%, Nasdaq up 5.19%). The board was broad, with 57 of 70 names higher and 13 lower, and 20 names finishing at or within 2% of a 30-day high. The trigger was the July jobs report: employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs and May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000, which pushed the odds of a September rate hike down to about 42% from 58%. Two blocks are still older than Friday by design. The macro chips come from FRED, which publishes with a lag, so the 10-year chip reads 4.69% from Aug 6 while the actual 10-year fell about 7 basis points on Friday to roughly 4.60% to 4.65%, and the oil chip reads $81.96 from Aug 3. CPI and core CPI are June data. The COT positioning section has finally refreshed: it is now the Aug 4 report released Friday afternoon, replacing the stale Jul 28 one, and it describes how institutions were positioned going into the jobs number rather than after it.

nextCpi.label: Next CPI print
nextCpi.delta: July data, 8:30am ET, and it is now the single most important number on the calendar. Friday's weak payrolls took the September hike from likely to a coin flip, but Fed Chair Warsh has been explicit that a hot inflation reading would put a hike back on the table. The energy setup helps: crude peaked near $86 Brent in late July and has been drifting lower since, and the FRED chip still reads $81.96 from Aug 3. June already showed real improvement, with headline CPI at 3.5% year over year (down from 4.2%) and core at 2.6% (down from 2.8%). A third consecutive cooling print would effectively end the hike debate. A hot one would reopen it two days after a record close.

nextFomc.label: Next FOMC
nextFomc.delta: This meeting also publishes the Summary of Economic Projections and the dot plot, so it carries more information than a normal decision. Friday changed the balance of risk around it: payrolls fell 23,000 in July, May and June were revised down a combined 103,000, and the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2% (a smaller labour force, not a stronger one). Market-implied odds of a September hike dropped to roughly 42% from 58% the day before. Remember the starting point: the Fed held at 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 in a 9-to-3 vote, its most divided since 2016, with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan all dissenting in favour of a hike. This is still a committee arguing about tightening, not easing.

top_picks.name: Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
top_picks.thesis: You like ETFs because you own the whole field without betting the farm on one company, and Friday is the cleanest illustration this monitor has produced. VOO holds the 500 largest US companies for a rock-bottom 0.03% fee. It closed at 710.71, up 0.61%, at a fresh 30-day high and about 3.5% above its 50-day average. The number that matters most is buried in the flow columns: VOO carried just one distribution day in the trailing window. Compare that with three for SPY, six for QQQ, seven for both semiconductor funds and eight for the technology fund. Distribution days count sessions of institutional selling on rising volume, so a reading of one against six or eight says the broad index is simply not the part of this market that institutions have been unloading. Underneath it, the week was violent in both directions again: Oklo rose 14.8%, Coherent 13.4% and Palantir 10.3% while Western Digital fell 3.8% to a 30-day low and SanDisk 3.7%. Owning all 500 turned that spread into a 0.61% gain.
top_picks.why_now: Because the market just repriced the single biggest risk to a long-term holding, and it repriced it in your favour. The September hike went from likely to a coin flip on Friday's jobs data, and the 10-year fell about 7 basis points in response. For an index that is roughly a third mega-cap technology, the rate path is the dominant input. The honest caveat has not changed and is worth repeating precisely because the news was good: at 100% of its 30-day range, this is a fine scheduled purchase and a poor opportunistic one. Nothing here is on sale. The quant work supports holding rather than timing: a 13.5% ten-year compound return, the best risk-adjusted return of the three at plain market risk (Sharpe 0.65), the shallowest historical drawdown at -32.1%, and roughly 23% odds of a down year.
top_picks.risk: A record high with a live September hike is the risk, and concentration is the other. VOO is about a third mega-cap technology, so the AI complex is a far larger share of your outcome than 'the whole market' implies. Friday's record came on thin volume (VOO traded at 0.85 times its average, the S&P fund at 0.88x and the semiconductor funds near half their normal volume), and rallies that thin are easier to give back than ones bought with conviction. The specific trigger to watch is the Aug 12 CPI print: a hot number puts the September hike back on and this index gives ground quickly. The other watch item is credit rather than equity, where the cost of insuring AI-infrastructure debt has been rising all summer.
sources: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq rise after July jobs report surprises to the downside
Treasury yields drop after surprise jobs loss in July

grade.note: Held at A, and Friday strengthened rather than merely maintained the case. One distribution day is the cleanest flow reading anywhere on this board, and it was earned during a week when the semiconductor funds accumulated seven each. The index absorbed a 3.8% drop in Western Digital to a 30-day low and turned in a record close. Best Sharpe of the three picks at plain market risk (0.65), lowest historical drawdown (-32.1%), a 13.5% ten-year compound return, and roughly 23% odds of a down year. The standing caveat keeps it from being anything other than a schedule holding: 100% of its 30-day range is the worst entry point in a month, so keep buying on a calendar rather than in one lump.

top_picks.bear_case: The bear case is that you are buying the AI capital-spending cycle at its peak without realising it, because the index label hides the concentration. Roughly $725 billion of hyperscaler capital spending in 2026 is holding up a large share of index earnings, that figure is up about 77% year over year, and a growing portion of it is debt financed rather than funded from cash flow. If capital spending plans are trimmed even modestly, the earnings estimates underneath a third of this index move with them. Add a hot CPI print forcing a September hike and you have both the numerator and the denominator working against you at a record high.

top_picks.name: Eli Lilly
top_picks.thesis: The reason this sits at number two is that it is the one holding on the shortlist whose fortunes have almost nothing to do with AI capital spending. Lilly closed at 1,185.71 on Friday, down 0.52% on a day when 57 of 70 names rose, which tells you exactly what it is: the ballast. The business case rests on the two GLP-1 franchises, which grew 91% and 123% in the most recent quarter and drove revenue up 48%, with full-year guidance raised to $85 billion to $87 billion. US market share widened to 60.9% against Novo Nordisk's 38.8% after Novo's CagriSema lost a head-to-head trial. The quant history is the strongest of the three: a 31.1% ten-year compound return, a Sharpe of 0.94, and the best reward-to-risk setup on the shortlist at 3.71.
top_picks.why_now: Because it is the least crowded thing you can own right now, and because sitting out a speculative Friday is a feature rather than a fault. While quantum names rose 12%, space names 10% and Palantir 10%, Lilly finished slightly lower at 67% of its 30-day range and only 2.4% above its 50-day average. That is a considerably better entry than the broad index at 100% of its range. The near-term calendar is the reason to pay attention now: public comments on the CMS Medicare drug price negotiation rule close on Aug 17, and the rule is expected to be finalised in the autumn. Policy headlines around that date are the most likely source of a better price.
top_picks.risk: Price and policy, in that order. This is a premium multiple on a franchise everybody has already identified, so the 31.1% historical compound return is thoroughly understood and unlikely to repeat from here. The policy risk is concrete rather than theoretical: Medicare negotiation is in its third cycle, negotiated prices for the first ten Part D drugs took effect on Jan 1, 2026 at discounts of 38% to 79%, another 15 drugs have been selected with prices effective in 2028, and Lilly's Trulicity was among those selected. The CMS proposed rule specifically targets high-expenditure biologics and fixed-combination products. Competition is the third risk, though it eased this quarter.
sources: CMS Issues First Proposed Rule for IRA Medicare Drug Price Negotiation

grade.note: Held at A. Friday added no new information, which for this holding is the point: it closed down 0.52% while the speculative end of the board rose 8% to 15%, and that non-participation is precisely the diversification you are paying for. The flow reading is unremarkable in a good way, at 67% of its 30-day range, 2.4% above its 50-day and four distribution days. What keeps it from displacing VOO at the top is not the business, which is excellent, but the combination of a premium multiple and a live regulatory process with a firm date on it. top_picks.bear_case: The bear case is that the GLP-1 franchise is priced as though it compounds at this rate indefinitely, and two things could break that. First, price rather than volume: Medicare negotiation, expanding international reimbursement scrutiny and eventual biosimilar entry all push realised price per patient down even as prescriptions rise. Second, the competitive respite may be temporary; Novo losing one head-to-head trial does not remove a well-capitalised competitor, and an oral GLP-1 from any credible entrant would reset expectations quickly. At this multiple, merely good growth is not enough.

top_picks.name: VanEck Semiconductor ETF
top_picks.thesis: This is the diversified way to own the AI hardware layer without picking which chip company wins. It closed at 582.70 on Friday, up 1.96%, and the case for owning the basket rather than the parts has now been demonstrated three sessions running from three different directions: it lost only 1.04% while AMD fell 7%, gained about 1% while Western Digital fell 11%, and on Friday rose 1.96% while Western Digital fell another 3.8% to a 30-day low. The fund is doing exactly what a basket is supposed to do. The underlying demand is not in question: roughly $725 billion of hyperscaler capital spending in 2026, up about 77% year over year, with Microsoft disclosing an $80 billion Azure order backlog it cannot fill because of power constraints.
top_picks.why_now: Because the technical damage is repairing rather than deepening, which is the change since the last briefing. Two readings moved in the right direction: distribution days fell from nine to seven, and the gap to the 50-day average narrowed from 4.4% below to 2.06% below. The fund now sits at 73% of its 30-day range, so it is neither washed out nor extended. That combination, a group that is still below trend while the index sets records, is where a scheduled buyer gets a better price than the headline suggests. The quant history is the strongest of the three on raw return: a 33.3% ten-year compound return and the best Sharpe at 1.01.
top_picks.risk: The group is still priced for very good news, and three consecutive earnings reactions have proved it. AMD beat and fell 7%, then SanDisk and Western Digital both beat and were sold hard, with SanDisk's guidance midpoint landing below consensus. When good results get sold, the bar is the problem, not the business. SMH remains below its 50-day average, which means the trend is improving but not repaired, and Friday's advance came on 0.52 times average volume, roughly half normal participation. The peer fund SOXX is worse still at 0.48x and 4.1% below its 50-day. Light-volume rallies in a group that has been distributed for weeks deserve scepticism.

SanDisk was up 469% and Western Digital 202% year to date before their reports, and both were sold on guidance despite beating, which is the classic signature of a cycle where the good news is already in the price. If NAND and DRAM pricing rolls over, the earnings that justify the whole group's multiple roll with it. The second leg of the bear case is financing: about a third of the $725 billion of hyperscaler capital spending is now debt funded, and the credit market has started charging more for it. Demand does not have to fall for the trade to unwind, only the cost of funding it has to rise.

top_picks_note: Not a buy list, a research shortlist. The three names are unchanged: one diversified core (VOO), one quality healthcare compounder outside the AI theme (LLY), and one diversified way to own the AI hardware layer (SMH). One grade moved: SMH goes from B- to B, because distribution days fell from nine to seven and the gap to its 50-day average narrowed from 4.4% to 2.06%, which is a trend repairing rather than a price rising. VOO and LLY hold at A. The pattern that keeps repeating is worth naming: three sessions in a row, a single-name blow-up (AMD down 7%, then Western Digital down 11%, then Western Digital down another 3.8% to a 30-day low) did essentially nothing to the baskets holding them. That is the whole argument for this shortlist, and the market keeps making it for us. The one uncomfortable fact to sit with: after a record close, the broad index is at 100% of its 30-day range, which is the worst entry in a month. Keep buying on a schedule.

insights.title: A record close with eight names being actively liquidated underneath it, and half of them are power companies
insights.body: This is the first briefing in a while where the flow data and the price data describe the same session, so read them together. On the surface Friday was clean: the S&P set a record, 57 of 70 names rose, 20 finished at or near a 30-day high, and there were zero heavy liquidation events across all 21 funds on the ETF shelf. Underneath, eight individual names carried a heavy liquidation flag, and where they cluster is the story. Four of the eight are in one section, nuclear infrastructure and power majors: Vistra, Southern, Dominion and Constellation. Vistra closed at the very bottom of its 30-day range with eight distribution days and volume 1.66 times average, and Southern also finished at a 30-day low on 1.44x volume. The other four are AMD, Western Digital (a 30-day low, 22.6% below its 50-day, 1.48x volume), Astera Labs and Novo Nordisk. The second thing to notice is how thin the rally itself was. On a record-setting day the semiconductor funds traded at roughly half their normal volume (SMH 0.52x, SOXX 0.48x), the technology fund at 0.71x, the Nasdaq fund at 0.75x and the S&P funds at 0.85x to 0.88x. Accumulated distribution has improved but has not cleared: SanDisk still leads the board at 11 days, followed by Intel, Vistra and MP Materials at eight, with VGT at eight and both semiconductor funds at seven, against just one for VOO.
insights.matters: A record close bought on half of normal volume is a weaker signal than the headline suggests, and the useful information for a long-term investor is not in the index level at all, it is in where the selling is concentrated. Right now that is power and memory, and those are very different situations. Memory is a cycle question (does NAND pricing hold), while the power majors are being sold as a proxy for AI capital-spending doubt even though electricity demand is a slower and more regulated business than the trade implies. The practical takeaway: keep the scheduled purchase in the broad index, since one distribution day at VOO says institutions are not selling it. If you want to be opportunistic, the discount is in the regulated power names, where Vistra, Southern, Entergy, PSEG and Dominion all sit at or near the bottom of their 30-day ranges. Buy those in pieces rather than at once, because eight distribution days at Vistra means the selling is not necessarily finished.
sources: How major US stock indexes fared Friday 8/7/2026
Vistra slides as AI-power names weaken and no fresh company catalyst emerges

insights.title: The economy lost jobs in July, and that is why the market had its best week since April
insights.body: July payrolls fell by 23,000 against expectations of a gain, and the previous two months were revised down by a combined 103,000, which is the larger number of the two. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2%, but that reflects a smaller labour force rather than more hiring. Bonds moved first: the 10-year yield fell about 7 basis points to roughly 4.60% before settling near 4.65%, and the odds of a September rate hike dropped to about 42% from 58% the day before. Equities followed, and the S&P closed at a record 7,757.64 to finish its strongest week since April, up 3.58%, with the Nasdaq up 5.19%. Note the direction of the debate, because it is unusual: this Fed is arguing about whether to raise rates, not cut them. It held at 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 in a 9-to-3 vote, its most divided since 2016, with three governors dissenting in favour of a hike, and Chair Warsh has said he would be prepared to hike in September if inflation runs hot. The macro chips on this page come from FRED and lag, so the 10-year chip still reads 4.69% from Aug 6 and the oil chip $81.96 from Aug 3.
insights.matters: The market is now trading a genuine two-sided macro setup, and Aug 12 resolves a large part of it. Weak employment argues against a hike; the inflation print argues either way. For a long-term investor the important point is that a bad jobs number was received as good news, which is a sign that rates, not earnings, are still the dominant variable for index-level returns. That has two practical consequences. First, do not read Friday's record as a verdict on business fundamentals; it was a verdict on the discount rate. Second, the groups that benefit most from lower yields are precisely the ones sitting at the bottom of their ranges right now: the regulated utilities in section 08 (Dominion, Southern, PSEG, Entergy all near 30-day lows) are rate-sensitive by construction. If the Aug 12 CPI print comes in soft, that is where the repair should show up first. If it comes in hot, the broad index at 100% of its range is the more exposed position.
sources: US stocks jump as employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs, raising hopes that rate hikes can wait
Treasury Yields Fall Sharply After Weak Jobs Report

insights.title: Memory is the only group that did not participate, and the round trip there has been brutal
insights.body: On a day when 57 of 70 names rose, the two worst performers on the board were Western Digital, down 3.81%, and SanDisk, down 3.68%. Both are now genuinely broken on the flow data. Western Digital finished at the absolute bottom of its 30-day range, 22.61% below its 50-day average, with a heavy liquidation flag and volume 1.48 times normal. SanDisk carries 11 distribution days, the highest count anywhere on either sheet, and trades 28.19% below its 50-day. The cause is now well documented: both companies beat on their fiscal fourth quarter, but SanDisk guided first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue to $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion, a midpoint below the $10.8 billion consensus, and the market decided that was enough. The context explains the violence of the reaction: heading into those reports SanDisk was up about 469% year to date and Western Digital about 202%. The damage spread internationally, with SK Hynix down roughly 10% and Samsung nearly 6%. Micron has held up far better, down just 0.44% on Friday at 55% of its 30-day range, though it too carries six distribution days and sits 9.62% below its 50-day.
insights.matters: This is what it looks like when a cycle stock stops being priced on this year's earnings and starts being priced on next year's, and it is a useful lesson to internalise before it happens in a group you own. Nothing about NAND demand collapsed; the guidance simply failed to clear a bar set by a 469% run. For a long-term investor there are two honest readings and you should pick one deliberately. If you believe AI storage demand is structural, this is a 22% to 28% discount to the 50-day average in the exact part of the chain that was strongest, and the way to act on it is small, scheduled purchases over weeks, not a lump. If you would rather not adjudicate the NAND pricing cycle at all, own it through SMH, where memory is a modest weight and the basket rose 1.96% on the same day these two fell. That is the case for the fund over the stock, made about as clearly as it can be made.
sources: Memory Stocks Slammed as Western Digital and SanDisk Outlooks Trigger Sector-Wide Profit-Taking
Sandisk, Western Digital Sink as Memory Chips Sell Off Despite Earnings Beats

insights.title: The nuclear sheet split in two: the developers ripped and the actual power companies were liquidated
insights.body: Friday produced one of the sharpest internal divergences this monitor has recorded. On the speculative sheet, Oklo rose 14.77% on 2.47 times average volume, the heaviest volume anywhere on the board, after its Groves Isotope Test Reactor achieved first criticality on Aug 6 and second-quarter revenue came in at $1.2 million against expectations of about $83,800. It still lost $48.5 million in the quarter, or $0.28 a share, and holds roughly $3 billion of cash. Centrus rose 7.49%, NuScale 3.70% and Nano Nuclear 7.04%, and the uranium funds followed, with URA up 3.96% on 1.15x volume and NLR up 3.47%. Meanwhile the established sheet went the other way. Vistra fell 0.56% to a 30-day low with a heavy liquidation flag, eight distribution days and 1.66x volume. Southern also closed at a 30-day low with a heavy flag. Entergy sits at 7% of its 30-day range, PSEG at 11% with seven distribution days, and Dominion at 12% with its own heavy flag. Constellation and Cameco were the exceptions, up 3.37% and 4.03%, with Cameco at a 30-day high.
insights.matters: The money moved from companies that currently sell electricity to companies that hope to one day generate it, which is close to the definition of a speculative rotation and worth treating with suspicion. Oklo's first criticality is a real technical milestone and it does change the company from purely pre-revenue to something demonstrable, but $1.2 million of revenue against a $48.5 million quarterly loss is not a business yet, and the stock still carries seven distribution days and trades 5.57% below its 50-day despite the 15% day. The more interesting long-term opportunity is on the other side of the divergence. Regulated utilities with real earnings are being sold to the bottom of their ranges partly because they are rate-sensitive and partly as a proxy for AI capital-spending doubt, even though the demand picture is intact (Vistra guides to 5% to 6% annual load growth in Texas through 2030, and US power consumption is expected to set records in 2026 and 2027). The practical takeaway: if you want nuclear exposure for a decade rather than a quarter, the discount is in section 08, not on the speculative sheet. Add in pieces, because eight distribution days at Vistra says institutional selling has not finished.
sources: Why is Oklo stock surging today?
Vistra Earnings Offer Window Into Power Generation Ramp-Up for AI Data Centers

insights.title: Photonics was the best section on the board again, and this time real volume showed up behind it
insights.body: The photonics and optical interconnect section, split out of fiber optics on Aug 4, has quickly become the strongest group on either sheet. Coherent rose 13.44% on 2.12 times average volume and closed at a 30-day high, 10.54% above its 50-day average, which is the second-most extended reading on the board. Applied Optoelectronics gained 9.19% on 2.44x volume, also at a 30-day high, and Credo added 8.45%, with Lumentum and Fabrinet participating. Coherent is now up roughly 41% over the week. Two things are driving it. The first is policy: a draft US proposal would restrict imports of new Chinese optical transceivers, and the FCC is preparing to enact a ban on new Chinese transceiver models, which hands the addressable market directly to Western suppliers. The second is demand, with Coherent's most recent quarter showing revenue up 21% year over year and datacenter and communications contributing 75% of sales. Its fiscal fourth-quarter report lands on Aug 12, the same morning as the CPI print.
insights.matters: The distinction that matters here is between a demand story and a policy story, because they behave very differently over a decade. The AI datacenter demand for optical interconnect is durable and does not depend on any government, and it is the reason this section exists on the board. The transceiver import ban is a policy trade, and policy trades round-trip: the same draft rule has already repriced these stocks in both directions more than once this summer. Coherent at 10.5% above its 50-day average, at a 30-day high, after a 41% week, and reporting earnings on Aug 12 is about as poor an entry as this board offers. The practical takeaway for a long-term investor is to want this exposure and to refuse to pay this price for it. Either wait for the post-earnings reaction, or take the exposure through a fund where photonics is a component rather than the whole bet. If you already own it, this is a reasonable place to let it run rather than add.
sources: Applied Optoelectronics Zooms 13% Higher on Pivotal Quarterly Print; Coherent Advances 13%, Lumentum Adds 8%
Coherent jumps as investors weigh optical-networking policy tailwinds and AI demand

insights.title: The whole speculative sheet caught a bid at once, which is a sentiment signal rather than a news event
insights.body: Look at the top of Friday's leaderboard and notice how little of it is company-specific. Oklo rose 14.77% on genuine news. But IonQ rose 11.86%, Rigetti 8.53%, Intuitive Machines 9.85% and Rocket Lab 9.46%, and the catalysts there were an Argus broker upgrade of the space group and generic analyst enthusiasm for quantum, not results. Palantir rose 10.32% on 1.75x volume after Bank of America reaffirmed a Buy and raised its target to $255, building on a quarter that showed revenue up 93% to $1.935 billion and full-year guidance raised to $8.15 billion, with short covering amplifying the move. When rate-sensitive, long-duration, mostly unprofitable assets all rise 8% to 15% on the same afternoon, the common factor is the discount rate, not the news flow. That is what a 7-basis-point drop in the 10-year does to things whose value sits far in the future. Palantir now trades 29.72% above its 50-day average, by far the most extended name on either sheet, and IonQ, Rocket Lab, Intuitive Machines, Rigetti, Centrus, NuScale and Nano Nuclear all closed at 30-day highs.
insights.matters: Sheet 2 exists on this board so that speculative exposure stays small and clearly labelled, and days like Friday are exactly why that separation is worth maintaining. A group that rises 10% on a broker upgrade and a bond-market move can fall the same amount on the reverse, and the Aug 12 CPI print is a live candidate for the reverse. Note the internal warning signs even within the winners: Oklo carries seven distribution days and is still 5.57% below its 50-day despite a 15% session, and IonQ has seven distribution days while sitting 8.72% below its 50-day. Both rose hard while still being institutionally distributed, which usually means retail and short covering rather than accumulation. The practical takeaway is unglamorous: this is not the day to add to the speculative sheet, and if these positions have grown beyond the size you originally intended, a rally on a broker upgrade is a better place to trim back to that size than a selloff is.
sources: Stock Market Today, Aug. 7: Palantir Surges on Bank of America Upbeat View After Strong Earnings
SpaceX Rises 11%, Intuitive Machines Gains 9%, Rocket Lab Jumps 8% as Wall Street Gives the All-Clear on Space Stocks

insights.title: Healthcare sat out the rally, and the calendar says why: comments on Medicare pricing close Aug 17
insights.body: Healthcare was the quietest section on the board on Friday, and its internal readings are the most washed out outside of memory and the power majors. UnitedHealth closed at 10% of its 30-day range, AbbVie at 11%, and Eli Lilly finished slightly lower at 67% of its range while almost everything else rose. The exception was Novo Nordisk, up 2.81%, though it carries a heavy liquidation flag and sits at 41% of its range. The XLV healthcare fund rose 0.75%, well behind the technology and semiconductor funds, and sits 4.96% above its 50-day with four distribution days, which is a healthier trend reading than the price action suggests. The policy calendar explains the caution. Public comments on the CMS proposed rule for Medicare drug price negotiation close on Aug 17, with the final rule expected in the autumn. The programme is in its third cycle: negotiated prices for the first ten Part D drugs took effect on Jan 1, 2026 at discounts of 38% to 79%, and 15 more Part D and Part B drugs have been selected with prices effective in 2028. The proposed rule targets high-expenditure biologics and fixed-combination products in particular.
insights.matters: Healthcare is the part of this board with the least connection to AI capital spending, which is precisely why it belongs in a long-term portfolio that is otherwise heavily exposed to one theme. Friday made that case by omission: while the AI complex rose on a bond-market move, healthcare did nothing, and a position that does nothing on the good days is usually the one that does nothing on the bad ones too. The near-term calendar is actually helpful for a buyer. Regulatory deadlines reliably produce headline-driven weakness, and Aug 17 is a firm date on the calendar rather than a vague risk. The practical takeaway: if you have been meaning to increase healthcare weight, the fortnight around that deadline is a more likely source of a good price than a record-setting week in technology. XLV is the diversified way to do it; Lilly is the concentrated one, with AbbVie and Novo Nordisk as the cheaper, more contrarian options.
sources: CMS Issues First Proposed Rule for IRA Medicare Drug Price Negotiation

smart_money.intro: Where the large, well-informed pools of money are actually positioned, read from the three sources a private investor can legitimately see: weekly CFTC futures positioning, published reports of Goldman Sachs prime-brokerage flow (the desk data itself is proprietary, so this is press reporting rather than a primary feed), and disclosed policy and corporate spending. It is a timing signal, not a guarantee, and institutions are wrong regularly. Treat it as context for when to add to a position you already believe in, never as the reason to own it. One timing note this week: the CFTC data below is dated Aug 4, so it describes how professionals were positioned going into Friday's jobs report and record close, not after it.

items.title: Hedge funds cut technology at a record pace over the past two months, while running record gross leverage
items.body: Reported Goldman Sachs prime-brokerage data describes a firm-wide retreat from exactly the theme this board is built around. Hedge funds pulled back from US technology stocks at a record pace over roughly the past two months, with the cumulative reduction in market value totalling about 10%, the largest such retreat from the sector since the data series began more than a decade ago. Positioning in the mega-cap complex was pushed to its lowest point of the year, with a sharp reduction in both gross and net exposure. What sits alongside that is the harder number to square: gross leverage for the full prime brokerage book rose for a third consecutive year to the highest level on record by the end of 2025, and net leverage remains near three-year highs. So the money is heavily invested overall while being unusually light in the specific sector that has led the market.
items.matters: Two readings are possible and both are worth holding. The bullish one is that a record de-grossing in technology removes the crowding risk that made this theme fragile, and leaves a pool of underexposed professional money that has to buy back in if the trade keeps working. Friday's 5.19% weekly gain in the Nasdaq is consistent with the beginning of that. The bearish one is that record gross leverage means the system has very little capacity to absorb a shock, so an unfavourable CPI print on Aug 12 forces selling that is mechanical rather than considered. For a long-term investor neither reading changes what you own, only how you buy it. The practical takeaway: this is an argument for adding on a schedule and in pieces, since a highly levered book with light technology exposure produces sharper moves in both directions than the underlying businesses justify.
sources: Goldman Says Hedge Funds Sell US Tech Stocks at Record Pace

items.title: Fresh data at last: fast money bought volatility protection and deepened its index shorts into the rally
items.body: The CFTC report finally refreshed on Friday afternoon, moving from the stale Jul 28 reading to Aug 4. The single largest change is in VIX futures, where leveraged funds flipped from a net short of 12,289 contracts to a net long of 3,773, a swing of 16,062 contracts in one week and the biggest positioning move anywhere in the report. They bought that protection when the VIX was sitting near 15, which is to say cheaply. At the same time they deepened their index shorts: the S&P e-mini net short widened by 32,523 contracts to 329,999 (having covered 25,389 the week before), and the Nasdaq-100 net short widened by 20,035 to 78,333. Asset managers, the slower long-only money, trimmed in both, cutting 7,737 contracts in the S&P (to 44.3% of open interest from 47.6%) and 12,400 in the Nasdaq (to 21.2% from 26.0%). Open interest in the S&P contract jumped from 1.98 million to 2.12 million. In the 10-year note, leveraged funds added another 75,931 to a net short of 2.23 million contracts, the familiar basis-trade position.
items.matters: The timing is the whole point. This snapshot is dated Tuesday Aug 4, three days before the jobs report and the record close, so it shows professionals hedging into strength rather than reacting to weakness. That combination (deeper index shorts, a flip to long volatility, and long-only managers quietly trimming) is what caution looks like in positioning data, and it sat directly underneath the best week since April. Two honest caveats. First, leveraged funds are frequently wrong and their index shorts are often hedges against long cash equity rather than outright bearish bets. Second, this data is four days stale and Friday may have forced some of those shorts to cover, which would itself explain part of the move. The practical takeaway for a long-term investor is narrow: professionals were paying up for insurance ahead of Aug 12 while the index made a record. That is a reason to keep purchases scheduled and modest, not a reason to sell anything.
sources: CFTC Traders in Financial Futures, report dated Aug 4, 2026

items.title: The $725 billion floor holds, and Microsoft says it cannot spend fast enough because there is not enough power
items.body: The four largest hyperscalers plan roughly $725 billion of capital spending in 2026, up about 77% from last year's $410 billion. The breakdown: Amazon around $200 billion versus $125 billion last year, Google $175 billion to $185 billion versus $91 billion, Meta raised to $125 billion to $145 billion from a prior $115 billion to $135 billion citing higher component prices and additional datacenter costs, and Microsoft $110 billion to $120 billion versus $90 billion. The disclosure that matters most for this board is Microsoft's: an $80 billion backlog of Azure orders it cannot fulfil because of power constraints. Operators across the industry say they cannot keep pace with demand for AI capacity. The counterweight, and it is a real one, is that a growing share of this spending is debt financed rather than funded from operating cash flow, which is why the credit market has become the place the buildout gets tested first.
items.matters: This is the number that decides whether the entire first sheet of this board is a durable investment or a cycle, and it is the reason the least glamorous layers are often the safest way in. Microsoft's $80 billion power-constrained backlog is the single most useful sentence in this section, because it says the bottleneck has moved from chips to electricity. That is a direct argument for the power section that the market spent Friday liquidating, and the divergence between the two is the clearest mismatch on the board right now. The practical takeaway: the demand evidence supports owning the picks-and-shovels layers (semiconductors through SMH, electrical and conduit, and the regulated power majors) rather than the speculative end. Watch the financing side as the thing that would change the thesis. Demand does not have to fall for this trade to unwind, only the cost of borrowing to fund it has to rise.
sources: Big Tech AI spending plans reach $725 billion
Hyperscalers Hit $700 Billion in 2026 AI Spending Plans

items.title: Two government decisions are actively moving prices on this board, and both have dates attached
items.body: The first is trade policy in optical networking. A draft US proposal would restrict imports of new Chinese optical transceivers, and the FCC is preparing to enact a ban on new Chinese transceiver models. That single draft rule is a large part of why Coherent rose 41% in a week and why Applied Optoelectronics gained 9.19% on 2.44 times average volume on Friday. It has repriced the same handful of stocks in both directions repeatedly this summer as the draft has advanced and stalled. The second is healthcare pricing. Public comments on the CMS proposed rule for Medicare drug price negotiation close on Aug 17, with the final rule expected in the autumn, and the proposed changes specifically target high-expenditure biologics, fixed-combination products and products that previously qualified for the small biotech exception. Separately, the GOV badges on this board mark names where the US government either holds equity (Intel, MP Materials, Lithium Americas) or is the anchor customer (Centrus, BWX, Rocket Lab, Palantir), and four of those seven rose more than 7% on Friday.
items.matters: Policy-driven moves deserve a different treatment from demand-driven ones, and mixing them up is one of the more expensive mistakes available to a long-term investor. A draft rule can be softened, delayed or reversed, so any price move that depends on it should be treated as reversible until the rule is final. That argues for patience with the photonics names at 30-day highs, and it argues for using the Aug 17 healthcare deadline as a shopping window rather than a reason to avoid the sector. The GOV badges cut both ways too: government backing lowers the risk of a company running out of money and raises the risk that its fortunes turn on an election or an appropriation. The practical takeaway: when a position on this board moves on a policy headline, ask whether the underlying demand changed. On Friday, in photonics, it did not.
sources: Coherent Corp. jumps 41% over the week as China optics restrictions coincide with earnings report
Key Facts About Medicare Drug Price Negotiation

primer.intro: A large AI data center is a machine built in physical layers, and money flows into it from the top (the customers who order it) down through every supplier who makes a piece. Here is where the dollars land, and why the least glamorous layers can be the safest way to invest.

sections.h: Start at the top: the customers
sections.p: The hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Oracle) announce the giant spending budgets, now roughly $725B in 2026, that everyone else competes to capture. Owning them is the most diversified way to own the theme, because their core businesses (ads, cloud, software) fund the AI bet and keep earning even if AI spending pauses. Two cautions: the market now scrutinizes the return on that capex, and roughly a third of it is now funded with debt rather than cash flow, which hands the bond market a vote it did not previously have. Meta's latest raise was attributed to higher component prices rather than more capacity, which is a cost increase dressed as an investment increase.

Nvidia (NVDA) designs the GPUs that do the AI math; AMD (AMD) is the challenger; Broadcom (AVGO) builds the custom chips hyperscalers increasingly design in-house, a trend now challenging Nvidia's near-monopoly. None own factories: TSMC (TSM) prints the chips using machines only ASML (ASML) makes, and every GPU needs memory from Micron (MU). Highest growth, highest risk, and the layer that falls first on any overcapacity or competition scare. It is also now the layer priced for perfection: AMD grew data-center revenue 107% and the stock still fell 7%.

Memory deserves its own line. Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron control over 95% of global DRAM and have shifted a large majority of combined output to high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators. That has sent AI memory pricing sharply higher and left consumer-grade memory scarce, which is a margin tailwind for MU, SNDK and WDC and a cost shock for every device maker. It makes this the most cyclical layer of the buildout, and the most crowded: about 16% of Goldman's prime-brokerage exposure was tied to AI memory names as of June 30, which is why guidance misses here move the whole group violently. The live fundamental question is efficiency: compression techniques that shrink the memory footprint of AI models could either soften the shortage or, by making inference cheaper, spread AI workloads widely enough to increase memory demand overall. SK Hynix is Seoul-listed, so US investors reach it mainly through the baskets.

sections.h: Layer 2: The box and the room
sections.p: The chips get assembled into servers by Super Micro (SMCI) and Dell (DELL). A rack of AI chips runs blazing hot, so it needs advanced cooling and power distribution from Vertiv (VRT), and fast switches from Arista (ANET) to connect racks together. This is the guts of the room, and these are project businesses whose revenue lands unevenly quarter to quarter, which is why single-day moves of 5% or more are routine here in both directions.

AI splits one job across thousands of chips, so they must talk at the speed of light over fiber. Transceivers and lasers come from Coherent (COHR) and Lumentum (LITE), contract manufacturing from Fabrinet (FN), long-haul interconnect from Ciena (CIEN), and the actual glass fiber from Corning (GLW). Optics content rises with every hardware generation as 800G gives way to 1.6T. This layer is now also a policy battleground, with a draft US rule targeting Chinese-made optical modules that has sent the group up 21%, down 2% and up 3% in four sessions without the rule itself changing at all.

The least glamorous and often most attractive layer: switchgear from Eaton (ETN) and Hubbell (HUBB), the steel and PVC conduit that carries every wire from Atkore (ATKR), jobsite supply from WESCO (WCC), transmission and substation build from Quanta (PWR), and the raw steel from Nucor (NUE). Physical, hard-to-substitute, multi-year backlogs. Four of these six names are sitting at or near the very top of their 30-day ranges, which is what sustained accumulation looks like.

A data center is useless without electricity, and AI has made power the true bottleneck. Existing-reactor operators signing long deals are Constellation (CEG), Vistra (VST) and Talen (TLN); the regulated fleet owners are Dominion (D), Southern (SO), PSEG (PEG) and Entergy (ETR); fuel comes from Cameco (CCJ) and Centrus (LEU); reactor and SMR technology from BWX (BWXT), Oklo (OKLO) and NuScale (SMR); and near-term gas-turbine and grid power from GE Vernova (GEV). Because the regulated names are effectively bond proxies, this layer trades against the 10-year yield as much as against the AI story, which is why it has been the weakest part of Sheet 1 while yields climbed.

Follow a dollar of capex: it lands most heavily on the chip layer, which captures the most dollars but carries the most risk (a rival can win a socket, custom silicon can erode the moat, and an overcapacity or return-on-investment scare hits it first). The power, conduit, cooling and fiber layers are lower-binary: whatever chip and model win, the building still needs steel, copper, transformers and megawatts. A newer distinction sits alongside that one: how the buyer is financed. Suppliers paid by hyperscalers with real cash flow are on firmer ground than pure-plays that borrow to buy chips, which is why the neoclouds trade on credit spreads rather than on demand.

macro_strategy.regime_label: A rate-driven melt-up: the best week since April was bought on thin volume, with professionals hedging into it and the selling concentrated in power and memory
macro_strategy.regime_detail: The quant model reads the market as an uptrend at normal volatility, and Friday's record close supports it: the S&P rose 0.62% to 7,757.64, the Nasdaq 1.30% to 26,690.62, and 57 of 70 names on this board finished higher with 20 at or near 30-day highs. Three forces define the regime. First, the driver is rates rather than earnings. July payrolls fell 23,000 with 103,000 of downward revisions to May and June, the 10-year fell about 7 basis points to roughly 4.60% before settling near 4.65%, and September hike odds dropped to about 42% from 58%. The assets that rose most were the longest-duration ones (quantum up 8% to 12%, space up 9% to 10%, Palantir up 10%), which is a discount-rate move, not a fundamentals move. Second, participation was thin. The semiconductor funds traded at roughly half normal volume on a record day (SMH 0.52x, SOXX 0.48x), the technology fund at 0.71x and the S&P funds at 0.85x to 0.88x. Third, the selling that remains is concentrated and identifiable: eight heavy liquidation events, four of them in the nuclear infrastructure and power majors section (Vistra, Southern, Dominion, Constellation) and two in memory, with SanDisk still carrying the highest distribution-day count on the board at 11. Underlying inflation continues to improve (June CPI 3.5% from 4.2%, core 2.6% from 2.8%), unemployment is 4.1%, the VIX is 15.15 and the 10-year to 2-year curve is positive at about 0.44 points. This is a genuine disinflation backdrop with a positioning problem layered on top, not a growth scare.

drivers.reading: A hawkish hold that just got less hawkish. Fed funds sit at 3.50-3.75% after the Jul 29 decision, held on a 9-to-3 vote with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan dissenting in favour of a hike, the most divided committee since 2016. Friday's payroll miss cut September hike odds to roughly 42% from 58% and pulled the 10-year down about 7 basis points to near 4.65%. The FRED chip on this page lags and still reads 4.69% from Aug 6. The 2-year is 4.25% and the curve is positively sloped by about 0.44 points, which is a normal, non-recessionary shape. Chair Warsh has been clear he would still hike if inflation runs hot.
drivers.playbook: Keep buying the broad index on schedule and let the rate path resolve itself, because you cannot forecast it and the committee itself is split three ways. Where rates do change what you buy is at the margin: rate-sensitive, dividend-paying assets are the cheapest things on this board right now, with Dominion, Southern, PSEG and Entergy all at or near 30-day lows. If you want to lean into a lower-yield outcome, that section is where the leaning is cheapest. Do not lean into it through the speculative sheet, which has already priced Friday's move in full.

drivers.reading: Genuinely improving, with one live test on Aug 12. Headline CPI fell to 3.5% year over year in June from 4.2%, and core to 2.6% from 2.8%. Energy has been the swing factor all summer: crude peaked near $86 Brent in late July and the FRED chip reads $81.96 from Aug 3, so July's print should carry an energy tailwind. The Aug 12 release of July data is the number that decides whether September is a hike or a hold, and it lands the same morning as Coherent's earnings.
drivers.playbook: Do not position for the print in either direction. What you can do is decide in advance what you would buy on a hot number, because that is the scenario that produces the better prices this board has been short of. The list writes itself from the flow columns: the broad index would come off 100% of its 30-day range, the regulated utilities would get cheaper still, and the extended names (Palantir at 29.7% above its 50-day, Coherent at 10.5% above) would give back the most. Have the shopping list before Wednesday morning rather than after.

drivers.reading: Cooling, and the market currently likes that. Employers cut 23,000 jobs in July against expectations of a gain, and May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000, which is the more meaningful figure. Unemployment ticked down to 4.1% from 4.2%, but that reflects a shrinking labour force rather than more hiring. Set against that, corporate demand in the AI complex remains extraordinary, with roughly $725 billion of hyperscaler capital spending planned for 2026 and Microsoft disclosing an $80 billion Azure backlog it cannot fill because of power constraints.
drivers.playbook: Watch for the point where cooling stops being read as good news, because that is the regime change that matters more than any single CPI print. The tell would be weak employment data arriving alongside falling equity prices rather than rising ones. Until then, the barbell that this board is built around still holds: own the diversified core (VOO or VTI) as the largest position, own the AI buildout through baskets rather than single names, and keep a genuine non-AI position (healthcare, dividend value) so that one theme does not decide your outcome.

drivers.reading: Cautious professionals, thin participation, and a record close anyway. The CFTC report dated Aug 4 shows leveraged funds flipping to net long VIX futures (a 16,062-contract swing) while deepening S&P shorts by 32,523 and Nasdaq shorts by 20,035, with long-only asset managers trimming both. Reported Goldman prime-brokerage data shows hedge funds cutting US technology at a record pace over roughly two months, about 10% of market value, while gross leverage sits at record highs. On this board, one distribution day at VOO against seven at both semiconductor funds and eight at VGT says the selling has been in the theme, not the market.
drivers.playbook: Read light positioning as fuel and record leverage as fragility, and let both argue for the same behaviour: buy in pieces, on a schedule, and do not chase strength. The specific instruction the flow data supports is to keep the broad index as the scheduled purchase (the flow reading there is the cleanest on the board) and to make any opportunistic purchase in the sections carrying the discount rather than the ones carrying the momentum. Right now that means power and memory, not photonics and space.

scenarios.trigger: If the Aug 12 CPI print lands soft and September is priced out
scenarios.response: The 10-year eases from the mid-4s and the rotation runs in favour of exactly what has been sold. The groups with the most room are the ones furthest below their 50-day averages and nearest the bottom of their 30-day ranges: the regulated utilities and merchant power names in section 08 (Vistra 9.4% below its 50-day at a 30-day low, Southern at a 30-day low, PSEG 4.6% below, Entergy 4.1% below), memory (SanDisk 28.2% below its 50-day, Western Digital 22.6% below, Micron 9.6% below), and chip equipment. The practical response is to have already been buying those in pieces rather than to start after the print, since the first day of that repair is usually the most expensive one.

scenarios.trigger: If the Aug 12 CPI print runs hot and September becomes a live hike
scenarios.response: The record close gives back quickly and the most extended names give back most. Palantir at 29.7% above its 50-day, Coherent at 10.5% above and the 20 names sitting at 30-day highs are where the air is. The broad index at 100% of its 30-day range has no cushion either. This is the scenario a scheduled buyer should quietly welcome, because it is the only realistic path to better entry prices in the near term. The response is to make the next scheduled purchase on time and slightly larger, not to wait for a bottom that will not announce itself.

scenarios.trigger: If AI credit spreads keep widening while capital-spending plans stay intact
scenarios.response: This is the slow risk and the one least visible in the equity price. Roughly a third of the $725 billion of 2026 hyperscaler capital spending is debt financed, so a rising cost of that debt can unwind the trade without demand ever falling. The names most exposed are the ones whose entire business is borrowing to build capacity, which on this board is the neocloud section (Nebius sits 15.9% below its 50-day already) and the pre-revenue developers on sheet 2. The response is to keep sheet 2 small, to prefer the layers that get paid regardless of who wins (semiconductors, electrical equipment, power generation), and to treat widening credit spreads as a more reliable warning than any equity chart.

macro_strategy.positioning: The stance is unchanged, and after a week like this the consistency is the point: a record close and the best week since April are noise against a ten-year plan, in the same way that three single-name collapses were noise against it. Keep the diversified core (VOO or VTI) as the largest position and keep adding on a schedule, noting that at 100% of its 30-day range this is a fine scheduled purchase and a poor opportunistic one. Own the AI buildout through baskets rather than single names, because the basket has now absorbed a 7% drop in AMD, an 11% drop in Western Digital and a further 3.8% drop to a 30-day low without meaningful damage. Keep a real non-AI position, which on this board means healthcare and dividend value, and use the Aug 17 Medicare comment deadline as a likely source of a better price there. Where you want to be opportunistic, buy the discount rather than the momentum: the regulated power majors and memory are the two places on this board sitting at the bottom of their ranges, and both should be bought in pieces over weeks rather than in a lump, because the distribution-day counts say institutional selling has not finished. Keep sheet 2 small and clearly labelled. Friday was a reminder of how fast it moves on a broker upgrade and a bond-market move, and moves like that run in both directions.

watchlist_notes: Two sheets, same columns. Sheet 1 is the established, large-dollar side across ten sections: semis and fab, chip equipment, memory and storage, servers and cooling, fiber optics and cabling, photonics and optical interconnect, electrical and steel, nuclear infrastructure and power majors, big tech, and healthcare. Sheet 2 is the smaller-dollar speculative side (nuclear developers and fuel, quantum, space and defense, government-backed materials and small AI infra, neoclouds). Read the Bull Score first: it is six checks on whether the long-term case holds, and hovering it shows which checks passed. No timing caveat this week, which is a change from the last two briefings: every price is a genuine Friday, Aug 7 closing print and every positioning column is computed from that same session, so the price and flow columns describe the same moment. What to look at first: the pos30 column shows how many names are stretched (20 at or near 30-day highs) against the handful at the bottom (Western Digital, Vistra and Southern at 0%, Entergy 7%, UnitedHealth 10%, PSEG and AbbVie 11%, Dominion 12%). The D-Days column is where the accumulated institutional selling shows: SanDisk 11, then Intel, Vistra and MP Materials at eight. The GOV badges flag names where the US government holds equity (Intel, MP Materials, Lithium Americas) or is the anchor customer (Centrus, BWX, Rocket Lab, Palantir).
